title: Severe iron deficiency anemia
summary: Admit symptomatic severe anemia, heart failure, syncope, hemodynamic compromise, inability to ensure treatment, ongoing blood loss or concern for alternate diagnosis.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit symptomatic severe anemia, heart failure, syncope, hemodynamic compromise, inability to ensure treatment, ongoing blood loss or concern for alternate diagnosis.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Vitals q4h when stable. Increase frequency or use continuous monitoring for hemodynamic instability, respiratory compromise, neurologic change, active resuscitation, procedural sedation, or rapidly evolving disease.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Cardiorespiratory status, perfusion, fatigue, bleeding history, diet and signs of heart failure.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Oxygen only for hypoxemia or cardiopulmonary compromise; it does not correct reduced oxygen-carrying capacity.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: IV access for unstable patients, transfusion or IV iron when specifically indicated.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: Regular diet and nutrition assessment. Avoid excessive cow's milk and address food insecurity or feeding disorder.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: CBC/indices, reticulocytes, ferritin with inflammation context, iron studies, blood film and targeted bleeding/malabsorption testing.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: Imaging is guided by suspected blood loss or another diagnosis; not routine for uncomplicated nutritional deficiency.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Oral iron is preferred for stable patients. IV iron or red-cell transfusion is reserved for selected severe/symptomatic cases and should be planned with hematology. Treat the source of deficiency.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Hematology, dietitian and gastroenterology/gynecology according to cause.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Monitor for heart-failure symptoms and transfusion reaction if blood is given. Provide administration/adherence teaching.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate chest pain, syncope, heart failure, active bleeding, hemolysis or unexpected failure to respond.

treatments.text: Oxygen only for hypoxemia or cardiopulmonary compromise; it does not correct reduced oxygen-carrying capacity. Regular diet and nutrition assessment. Avoid excessive cow's milk and address food insecurity or feeding disorder.
Oral iron is preferred for stable patients. IV iron or red-cell transfusion is reserved for selected severe/symptomatic cases and should be planned with hematology. Treat the source of deficiency.

title: Pediatric ischemic stroke
summary: Emergency stroke-team admission for acute focal deficit, speech change, seizure with persistent deficit, altered consciousness or high-risk arteriopathy/cardiac/hematologic disease.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Emergency stroke-team admission for acute focal deficit, speech change, seizure with persistent deficit, altered consciousness or high-risk arteriopathy/cardiac/hematologic disease.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Vitals q4h when stable. Increase frequency or use continuous monitoring for hemodynamic instability, respiratory compromise, neurologic change, active resuscitation, procedural sedation, or rapidly evolving disease.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Frequent neurologic checks, continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring, glucose, temperature and blood pressure. Document last-known-well time.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Protect oxygenation and ventilation; avoid hypoxemia and hypotension.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain reliable IV access without delaying urgent neuroimaging. Avoid unnecessary arterial puncture before anticoagulation decisions.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: Keep NPO until swallow safety is assessed. Use isotonic fluids and avoid dehydration, hypotonic fluid and glucose extremes.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Glucose, CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver profile, coagulation, type/screen and cause-specific cardiac, inflammatory and thrombophilia testing after urgent imaging.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: Urgent MRI/MRA when immediately available without delay; CT/CTA is appropriate when faster or hemorrhage must be excluded urgently.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Thrombolysis, thrombectomy, antiplatelet or anticoagulation decisions require immediate pediatric stroke/neurology/hematology consultation and are not determined by an adult default protocol.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Neurology/stroke team, PICU, hematology and cardiology/interventional neuroradiology as indicated.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Record exact onset/last known well and serial standardized neurologic findings. Maintain aspiration precautions.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate declining consciousness, new deficit, seizure, raised ICP, hemorrhagic transformation or airway compromise.

treatments.text: Protect oxygenation and ventilation; avoid hypoxemia and hypotension. Keep NPO until swallow safety is assessed. Use isotonic fluids and avoid dehydration, hypotonic fluid and glucose extremes.
Thrombolysis, thrombectomy, antiplatelet or anticoagulation decisions require immediate pediatric stroke/neurology/hematology consultation and are not determined by an adult default protocol.

title: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
summary: Admit suspected or confirmed CVST with headache, papilledema, seizure, focal deficit, encephalopathy or high-risk systemic disease; PICU for deterioration.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit suspected or confirmed CVST with headache, papilledema, seizure, focal deficit, encephalopathy or high-risk systemic disease; PICU for deterioration.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Vitals q4h when stable. Increase frequency or use continuous monitoring for hemodynamic instability, respiratory compromise, neurologic change, active resuscitation, procedural sedation, or rapidly evolving disease.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Frequent neurologic checks, headache/vision, seizure monitoring, hydration and signs of raised intracranial pressure.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Protect airway and ventilation during seizures or declining consciousness.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain IV access for significant illness, parenteral therapy, urgent investigations, procedural care or instability. Consider a second IV/IO during resuscitation.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: Use isotonic hydration and correct dehydration. Keep NPO until safe if consciousness is impaired.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver profile, coagulation, inflammatory/infectious workup and selected thrombophilia testing after acute management.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: MRI/MRV is preferred; CT venography is appropriate when faster or MRI is unavailable. Evaluate hemorrhage and raised ICP.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Anticoagulation is commonly considered even with selected hemorrhagic findings, but the decision requires neurology/hematology. Treat infection, dehydration and seizure triggers.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Neurology, hematology, PICU and infectious diseases/ENT when septic thrombosis is possible.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Serial neurologic and vision assessment; seizure precautions.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate falling GCS, new focal deficit, uncontrolled seizure, papilledema/vision loss, hemorrhage or herniation signs.

treatments.text: Protect airway and ventilation during seizures or declining consciousness. Use isotonic hydration and correct dehydration. Keep NPO until safe if consciousness is impaired.

title: Intracranial hemorrhage
summary: PICU/neurosurgical emergency for confirmed or suspected intracranial hemorrhage, significant trauma, focal deficit, seizure, declining consciousness or coagulopathy.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: PICU/neurosurgical emergency for confirmed or suspected intracranial hemorrhage, significant trauma, focal deficit, seizure, declining consciousness or coagulopathy.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Vitals q4h when stable. Increase frequency or use continuous monitoring for hemodynamic instability, respiratory compromise, neurologic change, active resuscitation, procedural sedation, or rapidly evolving disease.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and frequent GCS, pupils, focal examination and blood pressure.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Protect airway while avoiding hypoxemia and hypotension. Use neuroprotective ventilation targets with PICU guidance.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain two IVs/IO for instability and type/screen. Reverse anticoagulation/coagulopathy according to cause and protocol.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: NPO. Use isotonic fluids and avoid free water/hypotonic fluid. Maintain glucose and temperature.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: CBC, coagulation/fibrinogen, electrolytes, glucose, renal/liver profile, type/screen and cause-specific hematology testing.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: Urgent noncontrast CT for unstable acute presentation; MRI/vascular imaging after stabilization according to cause.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Manage raised ICP, seizures, blood pressure and coagulopathy using current neurocritical-care pathways. Definitive surgery/endovascular therapy is specialist-directed.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: PICU, neurosurgery, neurology, hematology and trauma/child protection according to context.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Head midline/elevated when appropriate, seizure precautions and clearly documented serial neurologic checks.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate any decline in GCS, pupillary change, Cushing response, recurrent seizure, expanding hemorrhage or coagulopathy.

treatments.text: Protect airway while avoiding hypoxemia and hypotension. Use neuroprotective ventilation targets with PICU guidance. NPO. Use isotonic fluids and avoid free water/hypotonic fluid. Maintain glucose and temperature.

sections.text: Admit inability to walk/feed safely, altered mental status, severe headache, focal deficit, opsoclonus, toxic exposure concern, raised ICP signs or uncertain diagnosis.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Vitals q4h when stable. Increase frequency or use continuous monitoring for hemodynamic instability, respiratory compromise, neurologic change, active resuscitation, procedural sedation, or rapidly evolving disease.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Serial gait/coordination, cranial nerves, mental status, swallowing and autonomic symptoms.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Give oxygen and escalate respiratory support only when clinically indicated. Reassess work of breathing, oxygenation and ventilation after every intervention.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain IV access for significant illness, parenteral therapy, urgent investigations, procedural care or instability. Consider a second IV/IO during resuscitation.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: Regular diet only after swallow safety is confirmed. Correct dehydration and hypoglycemia.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Glucose, CBC, electrolytes, toxicology/metabolic/infectious testing guided by history and examination. LP only after imaging when raised ICP is not a concern.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: MRI brain for focal/atypical findings, encephalopathy, severe headache, prolonged course or tumor/demyelination concern.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Supportive care for benign postinfectious ataxia after serious causes are excluded. Treat encephalitis, toxin, demyelination or tumor according to specialist diagnosis.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Neurology; toxicology, infectious diseases or oncology according to differential.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Falls and aspiration precautions. Document serial neurologic findings.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate worsening consciousness, focal deficit, seizure, persistent vomiting, papilledema or progressive ataxia.

treatments.text: Give oxygen and escalate respiratory support only when clinically indicated. Reassess work of breathing, oxygenation and ventilation after every intervention. Regular diet only after swallow safety is confirmed. Correct dehydration and hypoglycemia.

title: Acute dystonic reaction
summary: Observe or admit airway involvement, recurrent symptoms, severe pain, uncertain toxin/exposure, prolonged reaction or inability to ensure safe follow-up.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Observe or admit airway involvement, recurrent symptoms, severe pain, uncertain toxin/exposure, prolonged reaction or inability to ensure safe follow-up.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Vitals q4h when stable. Increase frequency or use continuous monitoring for hemodynamic instability, respiratory compromise, neurologic change, active resuscitation, procedural sedation, or rapidly evolving disease.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Airway, swallowing, neck/jaw spasm, ocular deviation, respiratory status and recurrence after treatment.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Give oxygen if needed and prepare for airway intervention with laryngeal dystonia or inability to handle secretions.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: IV access for severe or airway-threatening symptoms; mild cases may be treated by another appropriate route using the local protocol.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: Regular diet only after swallowing and jaw/neck function normalize.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Routine labs are not required for a classic medication-induced reaction. Obtain targeted toxicology/metabolic testing when diagnosis is uncertain.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: Imaging is not routine unless focal neurologic findings or another diagnosis is suspected.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Stop the offending dopamine-blocking medication and give an anticholinergic/antihistamine antidote according to the current local emergency protocol. Observe for recurrence.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Poison Centre/toxicology, psychiatry or neurology when severe, atypical or recurrent.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Airway and falls precautions. Review the full medication list, including antiemetics and antipsychotics.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate stridor, respiratory compromise, persistent symptoms despite treatment, hyperthermia/rigidity or altered mental status suggesting another toxidrome.

treatments.text: Give oxygen if needed and prepare for airway intervention with laryngeal dystonia or inability to handle secretions. Regular diet only after swallowing and jaw/neck function normalize.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Contact the Ontario Poison Centre immediately. Activated charcoal, serum/urine alkalinization and hemodialysis are indication-specific and must follow toxicology/nephrology guidance.

sections.text: Poison Centre/toxicology, PICU and nephrology early.

sections.text: Stop serotonergic agents, provide benzodiazepine sedation and active cooling. Cyproheptadine and intensive paralysis/ventilation are selected with Poison Centre/PICU.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Poison Centre/toxicology, PICU and psychiatry when intentional exposure.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Continuous temperature, rhythm and neuromuscular assessment. Avoid antipyretics as the primary hyperthermia treatment.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate rapidly rising temperature, severe rigidity, seizure, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, DIC or organ failure.

treatments.text: Oxygen and airway support as needed. Avoid physical restraint and prolonged struggle. NPO during severe agitation. Use isotonic fluids for dehydration/rhabdomyolysis and active external cooling.

title: Neonatal HSV infection / HSV encephalitis
summary: Maintain a low threshold for neonatal HSV, especially around the second week of life. Fever or hypothermia, seizure, lethargy, irritability, vesicles, CSF pleocytosis, thrombocytopenia, pneumonia, coagulopathy, or unexplained elevated AST/ALT should prompt HSV testing and empiric IV acyclovir; skin lesions may be absent.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit any neonate with suspected HSV. Use PICU/NICU for shock, apnea, respiratory failure, seizures, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, significant hepatitis, or multisystem disease.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Continuous cardiorespiratory and oxygen monitoring when ill, encephalopathic, seizing, or receiving respiratory support; otherwise frequent neonatal observations, temperature and perfusion checks.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Neurologic status, seizures, fontanelle, skin/eye/oral findings, urine output, hydration, bleeding, respiratory status, and progression of hepatitis/coagulopathy. Daily or protocol-directed CBC and renal function during high-dose acyclovir.

sections.label: Recognition pearl
sections.text: Median age in a large febrile-infant cohort was 14 days. Concern increases with age <21–28 days, seizure, ill appearance, temperature abnormality, vesicular rash, thrombocytopenia, CSF pleocytosis, prematurity, maternal HSV risk, or unexplained transaminitis. Absence of vesicles does not exclude HSV.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain reliable IV access immediately; consider a second line for unstable disease. Ensure hydration and monitor the IV site because acyclovir extravasation can injure tissue.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: Support hydration while avoiding fluid overload. NPO if significant encephalopathy, seizures, respiratory compromise, or aspiration risk; otherwise feed as clinically safe.

sections.label: Labs / microbiology
sections.text: Before therapy when this does not delay treatment: CSF cell count, glucose, protein, bacterial culture and HSV PCR; blood HSV PCR when disseminated disease is possible; surface/mucosal swabs and any vesicle PCR/culture; CBC/platelets, AST/ALT, bilirubin, INR/PTT, creatinine, electrolytes, glucose. Obtain bacterial cultures and treat bacterial sepsis/meningitis concurrently as indicated.

sections.label: Imaging / neurodiagnostics
sections.text: MRI brain and EEG when CNS disease, seizure, encephalopathy, focal findings, or persistent altered state is suspected. Do not delay acyclovir for imaging or lumbar puncture when unsafe.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Start acyclovir IV 20 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours promptly when neonatal HSV is suspected, adjusting for renal function and local neonatal pharmacy guidance. Treat SEM disease for 14 days and CNS/disseminated disease for at least 21 days. Continue empiric antibacterial therapy until bacterial infection is reasonably excluded.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Infectious Diseases, neonatology/pediatrics, neurology for seizures/CNS disease, ophthalmology for ocular involvement, PICU/NICU for instability, and pharmacy for renal dosing/hydration.

sections.label: Nursing instructions
sections.text: Strict intake/output; ensure adequate hydration; monitor creatinine and CBC/neutrophils; assess IV site; seizure precautions. Document all skin, eye and oral lesions and obtain specimens before they evolve when feasible.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: For CNS disease, repeat CSF HSV PCR near the end of therapy and continue IV acyclovir if still positive in consultation with ID. Escalate immediately for seizures, apnea, shock, rising AST/ALT/INR, hypoglycemia, bleeding, renal injury, or worsening encephalopathy.

treatments.text: Acyclovir IV 20 mg/kg/dose q8h with renal adjustment, hydration, CBC and creatinine monitoring; 14 days for SEM and at least 21 days for CNS/disseminated disease.
Obtain bacterial cultures and provide age-appropriate empiric antibacterial therapy while HSV and bacterial disease are being evaluated.

guidance: Canadian Paediatric Society: management of febrile young infants and prevention/management of neonatal HSV.
contentStatus: Clinical-support reference — verify neonatal dosing and local pathway

title: Hypokalemia
summary: Confirm the result and severity, obtain an ECG when moderate/severe or symptomatic, correct magnesium and the underlying cause, and prefer enteral potassium when safe. IV replacement requires a controlled infusion, verified concentration/rate, cardiac monitoring at higher-risk rates, and repeat potassium.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit symptomatic patients, K <3.0 mmol/L with ongoing losses or inability to replace orally, significant ECG changes, arrhythmia, paralysis/weakness, digoxin use, renal disease, DKA, or need for IV replacement. PICU for severe symptoms, arrhythmia, respiratory weakness, profound hypokalemia, or high-rate central replacement.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Vitals q4h when stable; continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring for severe hypokalemia, ECG changes, arrhythmia, digoxin toxicity, or IV replacement above routine ward limits.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Repeat potassium after replacement according to severity/route; monitor magnesium, renal function, glucose, acid-base status, urine output and ongoing GI/renal losses. Avoid drawing repeat samples from the infusion line.

sections.label: Severity / symptoms
sections.text: Interpret with the clinical context and local laboratory range. Symptoms may include weakness, ileus, cramps, rhabdomyolysis, palpitations and arrhythmia; ECG may show flattened T waves, ST depression, U waves, prolonged QU and ectopy.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Use enteral replacement whenever feasible. For IV replacement, use a functioning line and an infusion pump. Central access may be required for concentrations/rates above peripheral limits; pharmacy and local protocol must verify concentration and rate.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: Stop unnecessary potassium-wasting fluids/medications where possible. Encourage potassium-containing diet only as adjunctive therapy. Ensure adequate urine output before substantial replacement unless directed by nephrology/PICU.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Repeat a non-hemolyzed potassium if unexpected. Check magnesium, sodium, bicarbonate/venous gas, creatinine, glucose; consider phosphate, CK, urine potassium/creatinine, urinary chloride, renin/aldosterone, and toxicology/endocrine studies based on cause.

sections.label: ECG
sections.text: Obtain ECG for K <3.0 mmol/L, symptoms, cardiac disease, digoxin exposure, or planned IV replacement. Continuous monitoring for ECG abnormalities, severe hypokalemia, or higher-risk infusion.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Treat the cause and replace magnesium when low because potassium may remain refractory. Prefer oral/enteral potassium chloride for stable patients. IV potassium is a high-alert medication: dose, concentration, access type, and maximum rate must follow the current hospital pediatric electrolyte protocol and be independently checked; never give IV push.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Pharmacy for IV preparation/rate; PICU for severe/rapid replacement or instability; nephrology/endocrinology for renal wasting, recurrent or refractory hypokalemia, acid-base disorders, or suspected tubulopathy.

sections.label: Nursing instructions
sections.text: Confirm urine output, infusion pump, line patency, concentration and rate with independent double-check. Watch for infusion pain/extravasation and rhythm change. Do not administer potassium by IV push.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Recheck after each significant replacement cycle and before repeating. Escalate for falling potassium despite therapy, new ECG changes, weakness affecting breathing, oliguria, rising creatinine, or concurrent severe hypomagnesemia/hypophosphatemia.

treatments.text: Prefer oral/enteral potassium chloride when stable; IV potassium only by controlled infusion under the current pediatric electrolyte policy, with pharmacy verification and appropriate monitoring.
Replace magnesium if low, stop potassium-wasting therapies when possible, and address GI losses, alkalosis, insulin/beta-agonist shift, renal wasting or nutritional deficiency.

guidance: Current institutional pediatric electrolyte replacement protocol and pharmacy monograph.
contentStatus: Clinical-support reference — IV potassium limits must be verified locally

title: Hypophosphatemia
summary: Assess severity, symptoms, renal function and the cause. Prefer enteral replacement for stable mild/moderate deficiency; use IV phosphate for severe or symptomatic deficiency or when enteral therapy is not possible, with cardiac monitoring and close calcium, phosphate, sodium/potassium and renal monitoring.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit severe or symptomatic hypophosphatemia, inability to tolerate enteral therapy, refeeding syndrome, respiratory or cardiac weakness, hemolysis/rhabdomyolysis, neurologic symptoms, renal dysfunction, or need for IV replacement. PICU for respiratory failure, arrhythmia, seizures, profound deficiency, or unstable refeeding syndrome.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Vitals q4h when stable; more frequently during IV phosphate. Cardiac monitoring during intermittent IV phosphate per pediatric parenteral guidance.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Serial phosphate, calcium, magnesium, sodium/potassium, creatinine and urine output. Monitor for hypotension, tetany, paresthesia, seizures, edema and infusion complications. Recheck after replacement before redosing.

sections.label: Clinical features
sections.text: Weakness, respiratory muscle dysfunction, impaired myocardial function, irritability, confusion, seizures, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, rhabdomyolysis and impaired leukocyte function can occur in severe depletion.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Prefer enteral therapy when safe. IV phosphate must be diluted and infused slowly through a verified line using an infusion pump and pharmacy-prepared concentration. Avoid co-infusion with calcium-containing solutions because of precipitation risk.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: Treat malnutrition/refeeding risk and optimize enteral nutrition carefully. Do not rapidly increase calories in a high-risk patient until phosphate, potassium, magnesium and thiamine management are established.

sections.label: Labs / cause
sections.text: Check calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium, creatinine, glucose and acid-base status. Consider vitamin D/PTH, urinary phosphate handling, CK, hemolysis studies and nutritional assessment according to the suspected cause.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: No routine imaging. Obtain ECG or targeted imaging when symptoms suggest cardiac, respiratory, skeletal or rhabdomyolysis complications.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Use oral/enteral phosphate for stable patients when feasible. For IV sodium phosphate, CHEO lists pediatric replacement ranges of 0.08 mmol/kg (low), 0.16–0.24 mmol/kg (intermediate), or 0.36 mmol/kg (high) over 6 hours, with maximums and a maximum rate of 0.06 mmol/kg/hour; select sodium versus potassium salt based on serum potassium and follow the current local pharmacy protocol.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Pharmacy for product, mmol calculation, salt selection, compatibility and infusion rate; dietitian for nutritional deficiency/refeeding; nephrology/endocrinology for renal wasting, recurrent deficiency or mineral disorders; PICU for severe symptoms.

sections.label: Nursing instructions
sections.text: Independent double-check of dose in mmol, product concentration, diluent, line and rate. Cardiac monitor during intermittent IV infusion; monitor vitals and IV site; never mix or Y-site with calcium unless compatibility is explicitly confirmed.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Repeat phosphate and calcium after therapy and before redosing. Stop/escalate for hypocalcemia, tetany, hypotension, arrhythmia, oliguria, rising creatinine, hyperphosphatemia, or worsening neurologic/respiratory status.

treatments.text: Preferred for stable mild/moderate deficiency when tolerated; verify elemental phosphorus/mmol content because products vary.

Sodium or potassium phosphate selected by potassium level; CHEO pediatric ranges 0.08, 0.16–0.24, or 0.36 mmol/kg over 6 hours, maximum rate 0.06 mmol/kg/hour, with local maximum-dose and monitoring rules.

guidance: CHEO parenteral sodium phosphate monograph and current institutional pediatric electrolyte protocol.
contentStatus: Clinical-support reference — verify product concentration and local maximums

title: Refeeding syndrome
summary: Identify high-risk patients before feeding, measure and correct phosphate/potassium/magnesium, give thiamine, begin nutrition cautiously with dietitian guidance, and monitor electrolytes, glucose, fluid balance and cardiorespiratory status closely during the first several days.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit patients at meaningful refeeding risk who require nutritional rehabilitation, have electrolyte abnormalities, edema, bradycardia, hypotension, syncope, severe malnutrition, prolonged minimal intake, eating disorder instability, or significant comorbidity. PICU for arrhythmia, heart failure, respiratory failure, seizures, severe electrolyte derangement, shock, or rapid clinical deterioration.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Orthostatic vitals where safe, temperature and cardiorespiratory assessment. Continuous monitoring for severe malnutrition, marked bradycardia, prolonged QT, severe electrolyte abnormalities, arrhythmia, or IV replacement.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Strict intake/output, daily weight using consistent conditions, edema and fluid balance. Check phosphate, potassium, magnesium and glucose before feeding and at least daily initially; higher-risk patients may require q6–12h checks during the first 72 hours according to the local pathway.

sections.label: Risk factors
sections.text: High risk includes very low weight/BMI or rapid weight loss, little or no intake for several days, prolonged vomiting, eating disorder, malabsorption, oncology, chronic disease, postoperative state, alcohol/substance use in adolescents, or low baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain IV access for severe abnormalities, inability to tolerate enteral replacement, instability, or anticipated frequent bloodwork. Avoid excessive sodium/fluid administration.

sections.label: Nutrition / fluids
sections.text: Involve dietitian early. Start calories and advance according to the local pediatric malnutrition/eating-disorder protocol and individual risk; avoid an unmonitored full-calorie restart. Prefer enteral nutrition when safe. Limit unnecessary sodium and fluid loads and reassess for edema or heart failure.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Baseline CBC, electrolytes, urea/creatinine, glucose, phosphate, magnesium, calcium, liver enzymes; consider ECG, CK, uric acid, triglycerides, micronutrients and pregnancy testing based on context. Repeat frequency is driven by risk and abnormalities.

sections.label: ECG / imaging
sections.text: Baseline ECG for significant malnutrition, electrolyte abnormality, bradycardia, syncope or cardiac symptoms. Imaging is not routine unless heart failure, respiratory compromise or another diagnosis is suspected.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Give thiamine before or with initiation of nutrition according to the local pediatric protocol. Replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium proactively or therapeutically based on levels and risk. Do not delay urgently needed nutrition indefinitely, but slow/hold advancement and intensify replacement/monitoring if electrolytes fall or organ dysfunction develops.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Dietitian and the relevant admitting service; adolescent medicine/eating-disorder team when applicable; pharmacy for electrolyte/thiamine therapy; PICU, cardiology, nephrology or endocrinology according to severity.

sections.label: Nursing instructions
sections.text: Consistent weights, strict fluid balance, supervised nutrition plan where indicated, monitor edema, weakness, dyspnea, confusion and rhythm changes. Ensure all supplements and feed increases match the written staged plan.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Review electrolytes and clinical status before each major calorie increase. Escalate for falling phosphate/potassium/magnesium, edema, tachypnea, new oxygen need, heart failure, arrhythmia, neurologic change, severe weakness, hypoglycemia or fluid overload.

treatments.text: Baseline phosphate/potassium/magnesium/glucose, thiamine, cautious staged nutrition, fluid/sodium awareness and close monitoring during the first days.
Replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium using current pediatric protocols; slow nutritional advancement and escalate care when biochemical or organ dysfunction develops.

guidance: Current local pediatric malnutrition/eating-disorder refeeding pathway, dietitian and pharmacy guidance.
contentStatus: Clinical-support reference — individualized nutrition plan required

title: Pediatric cannabis ingestion
summary: Young children may develop profound somnolence, ataxia, hypotonia, vomiting, bradypnea or coma after edible THC. Admit until mental status, ventilation, ambulation and oral intake return to baseline.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Observe in a monitored setting for significant symptoms, uncertain dose, edible exposure, very young age or unreliable home monitoring. Admit for persistent somnolence, ataxia, repeated vomiting, hypoventilation, oxygen need or unsafe disposition; PICU for apnea, airway support, marked bradycardia/hypotension, seizure or coma.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Vitals at least q2h while symptomatic, then q4h when clearly improving. Continuous pulse oximetry for somnolence, bradypnea or oxygen requirement; cardiorespiratory monitoring for severe CNS depression.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Serial GCS/mental status, respiratory rate and effort, pupils, tone, gait when age-appropriate, hydration and urine output. Reassess after sleep and before discharge because effects from edibles may be prolonged.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Position airway, suction and provide oxygen as needed. Use bag-mask ventilation and definitive airway management for inadequate ventilation; do not rely on stimulation alone.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain IV access for moderate/severe symptoms, poor intake, recurrent vomiting, hypotension, diagnostic uncertainty or possible co-ingestion.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: NPO while significantly drowsy or aspiration risk. Resume oral fluids only when awake with safe swallowing; use isotonic IV fluids if dehydrated or unable to drink.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Check bedside glucose in altered patients. Additional VBG, electrolytes, acetaminophen/salicylate levels and targeted toxicology tests are based on severity, intentional exposure or co-ingestion concern; urine cannabinoid testing may support exposure but does not quantify severity.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: No routine imaging. Consider neuroimaging only for trauma, focal findings, unexplained coma or an alternative diagnosis.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Medications/treatments: Acute pediatric cannabis ingestion is treated primarily with supportive care; there is no specific antidote. Treat hypoglycemia, seizures and hypotension conventionally. Ondansetron may be used for vomiting after ECG/electrolyte risk review, but persistent cyclic vomiting in an adolescent with chronic cannabis use should trigger the separate CHS pathway. Avoid routine naloxone unless opioid exposure is plausible; a response does not confirm cannabis as the sole exposure.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Call the Ontario Poison Centre. Involve PICU for respiratory depression or severe CNS effects; social work/child protection when storage, supervision or deliberate administration raises safeguarding concerns.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Aspiration precautions, continuous oxygen monitoring when sedated, document neurologic trend and respiratory rate, and keep potentially contaminated packaging for identification.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate immediately for decreasing respiratory rate, apnea, rising CO2, recurrent emesis with reduced consciousness, seizure, persistent hypotension or failure to improve. Discharge only when mental status, gait, ventilation and oral intake are back to baseline with a safe caregiver plan.

treatments.text: Position airway, suction and provide oxygen as needed. Use bag-mask ventilation and definitive airway management for inadequate ventilation; do not rely on stimulation alone. NPO while significantly drowsy or aspiration risk. Resume oral fluids only when awake with safe swallowing; use isotonic IV fluids if dehydrated or unable to drink.

Medications/treatments: Acute pediatric cannabis ingestion is treated primarily with supportive care; there is no specific antidote. Treat hypoglycemia, seizures and hypotension conventionally. Ondansetron may be used for vomiting after ECG/electrolyte risk review, but persistent cyclic vomiting in an adolescent with chronic cannabis use should trigger the separate CHS pathway. Avoid routine naloxone unless opioid exposure is plausible; a response does not confirm cannabis as the sole exposure.

guidance: Ontario Poison Centre recommendations for pediatric cannabis exposures and current local supportive-care pathway.

title: Beta-blocker overdose
summary: Beta-blocker toxicity can cause bradycardia, hypotension, hypoglycemia, conduction disturbance, seizure and cardiogenic shock. Early Poison Centre and PICU involvement is essential.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit all symptomatic or intentional exposures and significant/uncertain pediatric ingestions to a monitored setting. PICU for bradycardia, hypotension, conduction abnormality, altered mental status, seizure, hypoglycemia, vasopressor need or high-dose insulin therapy.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and frequent blood pressure cycling; q5-15 min during instability or active resuscitation, then at least q1h until stable.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Serial perfusion, mental status, urine output and ECG. Bedside glucose q1h initially in symptomatic children or during high-dose insulin, then space only after stable.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Provide oxygen and early ventilatory support for shock, seizure or reduced consciousness. Avoid delays in airway management when perfusion or mental status is worsening.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain two IV/IO lines in significant toxicity. Consider arterial and central access in refractory shock with PICU.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: NPO during instability. Give cautious isotonic boluses with frequent reassessment because myocardial depression may limit fluid tolerance; add dextrose for hypoglycemia or during insulin therapy.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Baseline and serial glucose, VBG/ABG, lactate, electrolytes including potassium, magnesium and calcium, renal function and targeted drug levels when available. Repeat q1h during high-dose insulin initiation/titration and according to Poison Centre/PICU thereafter.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: No routine imaging; chest radiograph or bedside cardiac ultrasound may assist if pulmonary edema, aspiration or shock is present.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Call Poison Centre immediately. Initial therapy may include atropine for symptomatic bradycardia, glucagon, vasopressors and high-dose insulin euglycemia therapy; exact dosing and sequencing must follow the Ontario Poison Centre beta-blocker algorithm and local PICU/pharmacy protocol. Treat seizures with benzodiazepines; consider sodium bicarbonate for propranolol-associated QRS widening and lipid emulsion only when toxicology recommends.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Poison Centre, PICU, pharmacy and cardiology for severe conduction disease or refractory shock; ECMO-capable centre discussion for refractory cardiovascular collapse.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Continuous rhythm monitoring, frequent glucose and potassium checks during insulin therapy, strict intake/output and immediate reporting of bradycardia, hypotension, QRS widening or neurologic decline.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate rapidly for falling blood pressure, worsening bradycardia, QRS widening, rising lactate, hypoglycemia, reduced urine output or altered mental status. Refractory shock requires multi-agent therapy directed by toxicology/PICU.

treatments.text: Provide oxygen and early ventilatory support for shock, seizure or reduced consciousness. Avoid delays in airway management when perfusion or mental status is worsening. NPO during instability. Give cautious isotonic boluses with frequent reassessment because myocardial depression may limit fluid tolerance; add dextrose for hypoglycemia or during insulin therapy.

Treat seizures with benzodiazepines; consider sodium bicarbonate for propranolol-associated QRS widening and lipid emulsion only when toxicology recommends.

title: Calcium-channel blocker overdose
summary: Calcium-channel blocker poisoning may produce delayed severe vasodilatory or cardiogenic shock, bradycardia, hyperglycemia and metabolic acidosis.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit all intentional, symptomatic, modified-release or potentially significant ingestions. PICU for hypotension, bradycardia, conduction abnormality, hyperglycemia with toxicity, acidosis, pulmonary edema or need for calcium, vasopressor or high-dose insulin therapy.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and frequent blood pressure checks; q5-15 min during instability, then q1h while high risk.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Serial perfusion, mental status, urine output and ECG. Bedside glucose q1h during significant toxicity or high-dose insulin; hyperglycemia may be a toxicity marker.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Provide oxygen and ventilatory support when needed. Anticipate pulmonary edema from toxicity and aggressive resuscitation; use bedside reassessment frequently.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain two large-bore IV/IO lines; arterial and central access for severe shock in PICU.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: NPO during instability. Use cautious isotonic boluses; avoid repeated unassessed loading. Dextrose-containing fluids are required with high-dose insulin according to glucose trends.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Serial glucose, electrolytes including potassium, ionized calcium and magnesium, VBG/ABG, lactate and renal function. During high-dose insulin or calcium infusions, check glucose and electrolytes at least hourly initially, then per PICU/Poison Centre.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: No routine imaging; bedside cardiac ultrasound and chest radiograph may help distinguish cardiogenic dysfunction, vasodilatory shock and pulmonary edema.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Call Poison Centre immediately. Treatment may include IV calcium, vasopressors and high-dose insulin euglycemia therapy; exact agent, dose and targets must follow the Ontario Poison Centre calcium-channel blocker algorithm. Consider whole-bowel irrigation for selected modified-release ingestions and lipid emulsion or ECMO only after toxicology/PICU consultation.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Poison Centre, PICU, pharmacy and cardiology; early ECMO-capable centre discussion for refractory shock.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Continuous rhythm and blood-pressure monitoring, hourly glucose/potassium during insulin titration, strict intake/output and surveillance for fluid overload or extravasation.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate for hypotension, rising lactate, worsening acidosis, bradycardia, pulmonary edema, reduced urine output or altered mental status. Delayed deterioration can occur, especially with long-acting products.

treatments.text: Provide oxygen and ventilatory support when needed. Anticipate pulmonary edema from toxicity and aggressive resuscitation; use bedside reassessment frequently. NPO during instability. Use cautious isotonic boluses; avoid repeated unassessed loading. Dextrose-containing fluids are required with high-dose insulin according to glucose trends.

Call Poison Centre immediately. Treatment may include IV calcium, vasopressors and high-dose insulin euglycemia therapy; exact agent, dose and targets must follow the Ontario Poison Centre calcium-channel blocker algorithm. Consider whole-bowel irrigation for selected modified-release ingestions and lipid emulsion or ECMO only after toxicology/PICU consultation.

guidance: Ontario Poison Centre calcium-channel blocker treatment and high-dose insulin algorithms.
contentStatus: Clinical-support reference — call the Poison Centre and verify current local protocols

title: Clonidine and alpha-2 agonist toxicity
summary: Clonidine/guanfacine can cause delayed profound somnolence, miosis, bradycardia, hypotension and respiratory depression that resembles opioid poisoning.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit symptomatic, intentional, extended-release or uncertain ingestions. PICU for apnea, airway support, recurrent severe bradycardia/hypotension, coma or vasopressor requirement.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiorespiratory monitoring while symptomatic; q1-2h vitals until clearly improving, then q4h.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Serial mental status, respiratory rate, blood pressure, heart rate, perfusion and urine output. Observe long enough for delayed effects with extended-release guanfacine.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Airway positioning, oxygen and assisted ventilation as needed. Respiratory support takes priority over attempting to fully awaken the patient.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain IV access for moderate/severe symptoms, poor intake, hypotension or uncertain co-ingestion.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: NPO while drowsy. Give cautious isotonic fluid for hypotension and resume oral intake only when alert with safe swallowing.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Bedside glucose; VBG, electrolytes, renal function, acetaminophen/salicylate levels and ECG for significant, intentional or unclear exposures.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: No routine imaging; evaluate alternate neurologic diagnoses if the course is atypical.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Supportive care is primary. Naloxone may be trialed after Poison Centre consultation in significant CNS/respiratory depression, but response is variable and airway support must not be delayed. Treat persistent hypotension with fluids and vasopressors as directed; atropine is reserved for clinically important bradycardia.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Ontario Poison Centre; PICU for respiratory depression or cardiovascular instability; mental health and safeguarding teams as indicated.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Aspiration precautions, continuous respiratory monitoring, document arousability and immediately report apnea, falling blood pressure or worsening bradycardia.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate for apnea, rising CO2, inability to protect airway, persistent hypotension, poor perfusion or failure to awaken as expected. Do not discharge until vital signs and mental status remain normal off support.

treatments.text: Airway positioning, oxygen and assisted ventilation as needed. Respiratory support takes priority over attempting to fully awaken the patient. NPO while drowsy. Give cautious isotonic fluid for hypotension and resume oral intake only when alert with safe swallowing.

Supportive care is primary. Naloxone may be trialed after Poison Centre consultation in significant CNS/respiratory depression, but response is variable and airway support must not be delayed. Treat persistent hypotension with fluids and vasopressors as directed; atropine is reserved for clinically important bradycardia.

guidance: Ontario Poison Centre–directed management of clonidine, guanfacine and other alpha-2 agonist exposures.

title: Sulfonylurea ingestion
summary: Even one sulfonylurea tablet can cause prolonged or recurrent hypoglycemia in a young child. Normal initial glucose does not exclude later toxicity.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit any symptomatic child and any significant or uncertain sulfonylurea ingestion for prolonged glucose observation. PICU for recurrent hypoglycemia, seizure, altered mental status, high dextrose requirement or octreotide infusion.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Vitals q2-4h; continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring for symptomatic hypoglycemia, seizure or altered mental status.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Bedside glucose on arrival and at least hourly during the high-risk period, after any low value, and during dextrose/octreotide treatment. Continue observation for recurrent hypoglycemia after therapy is stopped as directed by Poison Centre.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Support airway and ventilation during seizure or severe neuroglycopenia.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain IV access early because hypoglycemia can develop abruptly; use IO access if symptomatic and IV access is delayed.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: Provide age-appropriate oral complex carbohydrate only if fully alert. Treat symptomatic or significant hypoglycemia with IV dextrose; avoid relying on feeding alone for recurrent toxicity.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Frequent bedside glucose is essential. Check electrolytes, renal/liver function and VBG if symptomatic, recurrently hypoglycemic or medically complex.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: No routine imaging.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Correct hypoglycemia promptly with dextrose. Call Poison Centre for octreotide because dextrose alone can stimulate further insulin release and recurrent hypoglycemia. Exact octreotide dosing, route, repeat interval and observation duration must follow Poison Centre and local pharmacy protocol.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Ontario Poison Centre; PICU/endocrinology for recurrent or refractory hypoglycemia; social work for medication-access or safeguarding concerns.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Use a clearly timed glucose flowsheet; report any glucose decline, change in behaviour, diaphoresis, pallor, tremor or seizure immediately.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Repeat glucose after every treatment and continue frequent monitoring until stable off dextrose/octreotide for the Poison Centre–specified observation period. Escalate recurrent hypoglycemia or neurologic symptoms immediately.

treatments.text: Support airway and ventilation during seizure or severe neuroglycopenia. Provide age-appropriate oral complex carbohydrate only if fully alert. Treat symptomatic or significant hypoglycemia with IV dextrose; avoid relying on feeding alone for recurrent toxicity.

Correct hypoglycemia promptly with dextrose. Call Poison Centre for octreotide because dextrose alone can stimulate further insulin release and recurrent hypoglycemia. Exact octreotide dosing, route, repeat interval and observation duration must follow Poison Centre and local pharmacy protocol.

guidance: Ontario Poison Centre guidance for oral hypoglycemic exposure; local pediatric hypoglycemia and octreotide protocols.
contentStatus: Clinical-support reference — call the Poison Centre and verify current local protocols

title: Anticholinergic and antihistamine toxicity
summary: Anticholinergic poisoning can cause agitation, delirium, hyperthermia, urinary retention, seizures, QRS widening and QT prolongation.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit symptomatic or intentional exposures and any ECG abnormality. PICU for severe agitation/delirium, hyperthermia, seizure, QRS widening, ventricular dysrhythmia, hypotension, coma or need for physostigmine under monitored conditions.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Continuous cardiorespiratory and temperature monitoring in moderate/severe toxicity; q1h vitals until improving.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Serial mental status, temperature, pupils, skin dryness, bowel/bladder function, urine output and ECG intervals. Use bladder scan for suspected retention.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Provide oxygen and airway support for severe agitation requiring sedation, seizure or coma.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: IV access for symptomatic patients; two lines for severe toxicity.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: NPO during delirium or seizure risk. Give isotonic fluids for dehydration/rhabdomyolysis risk while avoiding over-resuscitation.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Bedside glucose, electrolytes, VBG, lactate, CK, renal function and acetaminophen/salicylate levels for intentional or severe exposure. Repeat ECG after treatment and until QRS/QTc normalize.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: No routine imaging; assess trauma or alternate causes when indicated.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Use benzodiazepines for agitation and seizures. Treat drug-induced QRS widening with sodium bicarbonate according to the Ontario Poison Centre algorithm. Correct potassium/magnesium for QT prolongation. Physostigmine may be appropriate for selected pure anticholinergic delirium but only after Poison Centre consultation, ECG review and exclusion of contraindications.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Ontario Poison Centre, PICU for severe toxicity and pharmacy for antidote preparation; cardiology for persistent dysrhythmia.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Low-stimulation environment, active temperature management, fall precautions, strict urine output and continuous rhythm monitoring.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate for rising temperature, worsening delirium, seizure, QRS widening, QT-related ectopy, hypotension, rhabdomyolysis or inability to protect the airway.

treatments.text: Provide oxygen and airway support for severe agitation requiring sedation, seizure or coma. NPO during delirium or seizure risk. Give isotonic fluids for dehydration/rhabdomyolysis risk while avoiding over-resuscitation.

Use benzodiazepines for agitation and seizures. Treat drug-induced QRS widening with sodium bicarbonate according to the Ontario Poison Centre algorithm. Correct potassium/magnesium for QT prolongation. Physostigmine may be appropriate for selected pure anticholinergic delirium but only after Poison Centre consultation, ECG review and exclusion of contraindications.

guidance: Ontario Poison Centre physostigmine, QRS-widening, QT-prolongation and toxic seizure/agitation resources.

title: Hydrocarbon ingestion or aspiration
summary: Hydrocarbons primarily cause aspiration pneumonitis; coughing, choking, hypoxemia and respiratory distress are more important than the swallowed volume.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Observe symptomatic exposures and any aspiration concern. Admit for persistent cough, tachypnea, hypoxemia, abnormal lung examination, radiographic pneumonitis or CNS symptoms; PICU for escalating oxygen or ventilation needs.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Continuous pulse oximetry while symptomatic; q1-2h respiratory assessment initially, then q4h when stable.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Work of breathing, cough, oxygen saturation, mental status and fever. Symptoms may evolve over several hours.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Provide oxygen and supportive respiratory care. Escalate to high-flow or ventilation based on gas exchange and fatigue.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Not mandatory when entirely asymptomatic; obtain for respiratory symptoms, poor intake, altered mental status or significant exposure.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: Do not induce vomiting. Keep NPO initially if coughing, vomiting or drowsy; resume intake after respiratory stability and safe swallowing.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: No routine labs in a well child. Obtain VBG/ABG, electrolytes and other tests for hypoxemia, respiratory distress, altered mental status or co-exposure.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: Do not obtain an immediate routine chest radiograph in an asymptomatic child. Obtain CXR for respiratory symptoms, hypoxemia or before disposition when Poison Centre recommends; early films may be normal despite evolving aspiration.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Supportive care. Activated charcoal is generally avoided because aspiration risk outweighs benefit. Antibiotics and corticosteroids are not routinely indicated unless a separate bacterial infection or other indication emerges.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Ontario Poison Centre; RT/PICU for respiratory compromise.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Aspiration precautions, frequent respiratory reassessment and immediate reporting of new cough, tachypnea or desaturation.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate for increasing oxygen need, fatigue, worsening chest findings, fever with clinical decline or altered mental status. Discharge only after the recommended symptom-free observation interval and safe caregiver instructions.

treatments.text: Provide oxygen and supportive respiratory care. Escalate to high-flow or ventilation based on gas exchange and fatigue. Do not induce vomiting. Keep NPO initially if coughing, vomiting or drowsy; resume intake after respiratory stability and safe swallowing.

Supportive care. Activated charcoal is generally avoided because aspiration risk outweighs benefit. Antibiotics and corticosteroids are not routinely indicated unless a separate bacterial infection or other indication emerges.

guidance: Ontario Poison Centre–directed management of hydrocarbon exposure and current pediatric aspiration-pneumonitis practice.
contentStatus: Clinical-support reference — call the Poison Centre and verify current local protocols
sourceLabels: Current local PICU, pharmacy and emergency pathways

title: Lithium toxicity
summary: Lithium toxicity may be acute, acute-on-chronic or chronic; neurologic symptoms and renal impairment may be severe despite only moderately elevated levels.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit symptomatic exposure, elevated/rising lithium concentration, renal impairment, dehydration, intentional ingestion or acute-on-chronic/chronic toxicity. PICU and nephrology for significant neurologic findings, dysrhythmia, severe level, renal failure or dialysis consideration.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Vitals q2-4h; continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring for significant toxicity or ECG abnormality.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Serial neurologic examinations for tremor, ataxia, confusion, hyperreflexia, clonus, seizure and declining consciousness; strict urine output and fluid balance.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Support airway/ventilation for seizure or severe encephalopathy.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Reliable IV access; two lines for severe toxicity.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: Correct volume depletion with isotonic saline while monitoring sodium and urine output. Avoid dehydration and medications that reduce lithium clearance.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Lithium concentration on arrival and serially, commonly q2-4h until clearly falling and then spaced per Poison Centre; electrolytes, sodium, calcium, glucose, renal function, serum osmolality, thyroid testing when relevant and ECG. Interpret levels with timing and clinical pattern.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: Abdominal imaging or whole-bowel irrigation may be considered for selected large sustained-release ingestions after Poison Centre consultation.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: There is no antidote. Stop lithium and interacting nephrotoxic drugs, provide isotonic fluid resuscitation and correct electrolytes. Hemodialysis decisions depend on symptoms, renal function, exposure pattern, level and trend; use the Ontario Poison Centre lithium algorithm with nephrology.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Ontario Poison Centre, nephrology and PICU; psychiatry after medical stabilization for intentional ingestion.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Frequent neurologic checks, strict intake/output, fall precautions and accurate timing of serial lithium levels.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate for worsening confusion, ataxia, seizure, rising level, oliguria, sodium abnormality or dysrhythmia. Rebound levels can occur after dialysis or sustained-release ingestion, requiring continued monitoring.

treatments.text: Support airway/ventilation for seizure or severe encephalopathy. Correct volume depletion with isotonic saline while monitoring sodium and urine output. Avoid dehydration and medications that reduce lithium clearance.

There is no antidote. Stop lithium and interacting nephrotoxic drugs, provide isotonic fluid resuscitation and correct electrolytes. Hemodialysis decisions depend on symptoms, renal function, exposure pattern, level and trend; use the Ontario Poison Centre lithium algorithm with nephrology.

title: Methemoglobinemia
summary: Suspect methemoglobinemia with cyanosis and low pulse oximetry that does not correct as expected with oxygen, especially after oxidant exposure.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit symptomatic patients and confirmed significant methemoglobinemia. PICU for dyspnea, altered mental status, acidosis, dysrhythmia, hemolysis, significant level or methylene-blue treatment.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiorespiratory monitoring; frequent blood pressure and neurologic assessment.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Assess cyanosis, work of breathing, mental status and perfusion. Pulse oximetry is unreliable for severity; use co-oximetry.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Give high-flow oxygen immediately, recognizing that saturation may remain near the mid-80s despite adequate PaO2. Provide airway/ventilatory support if clinically required.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain IV access promptly; two lines in severe cases.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: NPO if unstable; otherwise maintain hydration.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Urgent blood gas with co-oximetry/methemoglobin level, CBC, smear/hemolysis studies, lactate, electrolytes, renal/liver function and G6PD status if rapidly available without delaying treatment. Repeat methemoglobin level after therapy and for rebound, especially with long-acting agents such as dapsone.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: No routine imaging unless an alternate cardiopulmonary process is suspected.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Stop the oxidant. Methylene blue is first-line for clinically significant cases but dose, repeat dosing and contraindications must be confirmed with Poison Centre; use caution in G6PD deficiency and serotonergic co-medication. Alternatives such as ascorbic acid, exchange transfusion or hyperbaric oxygen are specialist-directed.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Ontario Poison Centre, PICU, hematology and pharmacy; consider transfusion medicine/hyperbaric service in refractory cases.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Do not titrate care to pulse oximetry alone; trend clinical status and co-oximetry. Watch for recurrent cyanosis and hemolysis.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate for worsening neurologic symptoms, acidosis, dysrhythmia, hemolysis or rebound methemoglobinemia. Repeat co-oximetry according to clinical response and Poison Centre advice.

treatments.text: Give high-flow oxygen immediately, recognizing that saturation may remain near the mid-80s despite adequate PaO2. Provide airway/ventilatory support if clinically required. NPO if unstable; otherwise maintain hydration.

Alternatives such as ascorbic acid, exchange transfusion or hyperbaric oxygen are specialist-directed.

title: Isoniazid poisoning
summary: Isoniazid overdose causes abrupt, refractory seizures and severe lactic acidosis; pyridoxine is the specific antidote and must be obtained immediately.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: PICU for any symptomatic or significant suspected ingestion. Even initially stable intentional exposures require monitored admission because seizures can be abrupt.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring with frequent blood pressure and temperature assessment.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Neurologic status, seizure burden, acid-base status, lactate, glucose and urine output.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Prepare for early airway control because seizures may be recurrent and severe. Provide oxygen and ventilation; treat hyperthermia.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain IV/IO access immediately and secure additional access for antidote and resuscitation.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: NPO. Use isotonic resuscitation and correct hypoglycemia/electrolytes; avoid excessive bicarbonate without toxicology guidance.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Immediate VBG/ABG, lactate, glucose, electrolytes, renal/liver function, CK and targeted co-ingestion tests. Repeat gases and lactate frequently during active toxicity, often q1-2h until improving.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: No routine imaging unless trauma or alternative neurologic pathology is suspected.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Give benzodiazepines for seizures and administer pyridoxine urgently. When the ingested INH dose is known, pyridoxine is generally matched gram-for-gram; when unknown, use the current Poison Centre weight-based protocol. Do not delay pyridoxine while escalating conventional antiseizure therapy. Exact preparation, maximum dose and repeat dosing require Poison Centre/pharmacy direction.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Ontario Poison Centre, PICU, pharmacy and neurology for persistent seizures; nephrology for severe refractory acidosis or renal complications.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Seizure precautions, continuous EEG when indicated, frequent temperature checks and ensure pyridoxine supply is physically at bedside.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate immediately for recurrent seizure, severe acidosis, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, hypotension or dysrhythmia. Continue intensive monitoring until seizures and metabolic abnormalities resolve.

treatments.text: Prepare for early airway control because seizures may be recurrent and severe. Provide oxygen and ventilation; treat hyperthermia. NPO. Use isotonic resuscitation and correct hypoglycemia/electrolytes; avoid excessive bicarbonate without toxicology guidance.

title: Digoxin toxicity
summary: Digoxin toxicity can produce vomiting, bradycardia, AV block, ventricular dysrhythmia, hyperkalemia and neurologic symptoms; serum levels must be interpreted with timing.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: Admit symptomatic, intentional or significant exposures and any ECG/electrolyte abnormality. PICU for dysrhythmia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, altered mental status or digoxin immune Fab administration.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring; frequent blood pressure checks during instability.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Serial ECG/rhythm, perfusion, mental status, vomiting and urine output.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Provide oxygen and airway support as clinically indicated; avoid hypoxia and acidosis that worsen dysrhythmia risk.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Obtain reliable IV access; two lines in unstable patients.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: NPO while unstable or vomiting. Correct dehydration cautiously and avoid rapid electrolyte shifts.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium and calcium, renal function, glucose, VBG/lactate if ill, and digoxin concentration drawn at an interpretable post-ingestion interval. Repeat potassium and ECG frequently in significant toxicity. After Fab, routine total digoxin levels are misleading.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: No routine imaging; identify plant/tablet exposure when possible.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Call Poison Centre immediately. Digoxin immune Fab is indicated for selected life-threatening toxicity; vial calculation and administration must follow Poison Centre/pharmacy guidance. Treat significant bradyarrhythmia or ventricular dysrhythmia with toxicology-directed agents. Avoid empiric calcium for hyperkalemia unless Poison Centre specifically advises.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Ontario Poison Centre, PICU, pharmacy and cardiology.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Continuous rhythm monitoring, frequent potassium checks, keep resuscitation equipment available and document timing of digoxin level relative to ingestion and Fab.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate for hyperkalemia, progressive AV block, ventricular ectopy, hypotension, altered mental status or worsening renal function. Monitor for rebound after Fab in renal impairment or large exposure.

treatments.text: Provide oxygen and airway support as clinically indicated; avoid hypoxia and acidosis that worsen dysrhythmia risk. NPO while unstable or vomiting. Correct dehydration cautiously and avoid rapid electrolyte shifts.

Call Poison Centre immediately. Digoxin immune Fab is indicated for selected life-threatening toxicity; vial calculation and administration must follow Poison Centre/pharmacy guidance. Treat significant bradyarrhythmia or ventricular dysrhythmia with toxicology-directed agents. Avoid empiric calcium for hyperkalemia unless Poison Centre specifically advises.

guidance: Ontario Poison Centre–directed cardiac glycoside poisoning management and local digoxin immune Fab protocol.

title: Toxic seizure or severe agitation
summary: Toxic seizures and severe agitation require rapid benzodiazepine treatment, temperature control, glucose assessment and toxin-specific therapy; phenytoin is often ineffective for toxin-induced seizures.

sections.label: Admission / disposition
sections.text: PICU for toxic seizure, recurrent seizure, severe agitation requiring repeated sedation, hyperthermia, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, dysrhythmia or airway support.

sections.label: Vitals
sections.text: Continuous cardiorespiratory, pulse-oximetry and temperature monitoring; frequent blood pressure checks.

sections.label: Monitoring
sections.text: Airway, seizure duration/recurrence, mental status, core temperature, glucose, ECG, urine output and signs of trauma or serotonin/anticholinergic/sympathomimetic syndromes.

sections.label: Respiratory support
sections.text: Position airway, provide oxygen and ventilatory support. Intubate when seizures are refractory, sedation compromises ventilation or severe hyperthermia requires paralysis.

sections.label: IV access
sections.text: Immediate IV/IO access; obtain additional access for antidotes and cooling/resuscitation.

sections.label: Fluids / diet
sections.text: NPO. Use isotonic fluids for dehydration/rhabdomyolysis while monitoring sodium and cardiac function.

sections.label: Labs
sections.text: Immediate glucose, VBG/ABG, lactate, electrolytes including sodium/calcium/magnesium, renal function, CK and targeted drug levels. Repeat gases, lactate and electrolytes q1-2h during active severe toxicity.

sections.label: Imaging
sections.text: CT head only when trauma, focal deficit, persistent unexplained coma or non-toxic cause is possible.

sections.label: Medications / treatment
sections.text: Benzodiazepines are first-line and should be repeated promptly. Correct hypoglycemia and electrolyte abnormalities. Use toxin-specific antidotes such as pyridoxine for INH, sodium bicarbonate for sodium-channel blockade or naloxone for opioid-associated hypoventilation when indicated. Avoid routine phenytoin for toxin-induced seizures unless a separate indication exists. Refractory cases require PICU/toxicology-directed anesthetic therapy.

sections.label: Consults
sections.text: Ontario Poison Centre, PICU, pharmacy and neurology; consider nephrology/ECMO based on toxin and organ failure.

sections.label: Nursing / RT instructions
sections.text: Seizure precautions, active cooling, low-stimulation environment, continuous ECG, strict urine output and rapid access to repeat benzodiazepine doses.

sections.label: Reassessment / contingency
sections.text: Escalate for recurrent seizure, persistent agitation, hyperthermia, QRS/QT abnormality, rising lactate, rhabdomyolysis, hypotension or worsening consciousness. Search actively for the responsible toxidrome and co-ingestions.

treatments.text: Position airway, provide oxygen and ventilatory support. Intubate when seizures are refractory, sedation compromises ventilation or severe hyperthermia requires paralysis. NPO. Use isotonic fluids for dehydration/rhabdomyolysis while monitoring sodium and cardiac function.

Use toxin-specific antidotes such as pyridoxine for INH, sodium bicarbonate for sodium-channel blockade or naloxone for opioid-associated hypoventilation when indicated. Avoid routine phenytoin for toxin-induced seizures unless a separate indication exists. Refractory cases require PICU/toxicology-directed anesthetic therapy.
